findings.summary: FinCEN issued a consent order imposing a $1.3 billion civil money penalty against TD Bank, N.A. and TD Bank USA, N.A. for willful violations of the Bank Secrecy Act and its implementing regulations, with $757 million payable to the U.S. Treasury after crediting $543 million for payments to DOJ and OCC.

The OCC issued a cease and desist order, assessed a $450 million civil money penalty, and imposed an asset cap and growth restriction on TD Bank, N.A. and TD Bank USA, N.A. for deficiencies in the bank's BSA/AML compliance program, including systemic breakdowns in suspicious activity reporting and currency transaction reporting.

The Federal Reserve Board fined Toronto-Dominion Bank $123.5 million and issued a cease and desist order for anti-money laundering violations and risk management deficiencies, requiring TD to establish a U.S. office dedicated to AML remediation and relocate its U.S. AML compliance program to the United States.

The CFPB ordered TD Bank to pay $7.76 million in redress to affected consumers and a $20 million civil money penalty for repeatedly sharing inaccurate, negative credit information with consumer reporting agencies, in violation of the Fair Credit Reporting Act and Regulation V.

The CFTC ordered The Toronto Dominion Bank to pay a $75 million civil monetary penalty and ordered it to cease and desist from violations of CFTC recordkeeping and supervision requirements for firm-wide use of unapproved communication methods from at least 2015 onward.

The CFTC ordered The Toronto Dominion Bank to pay a $4 million civil monetary penalty and cease and desist from further violations for failing to diligently supervise its electronic communications surveillance system, resulting in failure to surveil communications for hundreds of swap dealer personnel over a five-year period.

TD Bank, N.A. and TD Bank US Holding Company entered into plea agreements with the U.S. Department of Justice on October 10, 2024, with TD Bank, N.A. agreeing to plead guilty to a criminal violation of 18 U.S.C. § 371 and TDBUSH agreeing to plead guilty to criminal violations of 31 U.S.C. §§ 5322 and 5324, as part of a broader ~$3.09 billion resolution of AML investigations.

On June 27, 2025, Judge Renee Marie Bumb of the U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey dismissed a proposed class action (Stevens v. TD Bank) alleging TD Bank violated the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act by embedding a hidden Meta tracking pixel on its website that shared customers' personal financial information. The court ruled plaintiff Jefferey Stevens lacked standing because he failed to identify what data was captured or how Meta could identify him; the dismissal was without prejudice, allowing him to amend.

On November 3, 2026, Justice Janet Leiper of the Ontario Superior Court of Justice granted leave under Part XXIII.1 of the Ontario Securities Act and certified a misrepresentation class action against The Toronto-Dominion Bank and several senior officers/directors (including former CEO Bharat Masrani). The action alleges TD misrepresented the effectiveness of its anti-money laundering controls and the existence of criminal/regulatory investigations between 2021 and 2024, causing a CA$30 billion drop in market capitalization and investor losses.

On October 15, 2024, the U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey granted final approval of a $32,225,000 class action settlement in Burns v. TD Bank, N.A. (Case No. 1:21-cv-18194), resolving claims that TD Bank improperly assessed APSN overdraft fees on transactions authorized when the available balance was positive. Settlement payments to class members began in March 2025. TD Bank denied wrongdoing.

On October 2, 2025, a proposed class action (Trisal v. TD Bank, N.A., No. 1:25-cv-16196) was filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey alleging TD Bank unlawfully assessed unrefunded $35 overdraft fees on accounts whose holders cured the overdraft by the next business day. The suit was terminated on May 15, 2026.

On February 15, 2024, the Ontario Superior Court of Justice approved a settlement in the Tyler Dufault v. The Toronto-Dominion Bank class action, resolving claims that TD Bank charged non-sufficient funds fees on re-presented pre-authorized debit transactions between February 2, 2019 and November 27, 2023. The plaintiff had previously succeeded on a motion for summary judgment against TD Bank.

On October 13, 2026, Judge Arun Subramanian of the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York partially denied defendants' motion to dismiss in Tiessen v. The Toronto-Dominion Bank (Case No. 24-cv-8032), a securities fraud class action alleging TD made misrepresentations about its Bank Secrecy Act/AML controls. The case proceeds to discovery.

On January 31, 2025, lead plaintiffs in In re TD Bank / First Horizon Securities Litigation (Case No. 23-02763, D.N.J.) filed a Third Amended Consolidated Class Action Complaint on behalf of purchasers of First Horizon Corporation securities between February 28, 2022 and May 3, 2023, alleging misrepresentations concerning TD Bank's AML compliance and its proposed acquisition of First Horizon, which regulators refused to approve due to concealed AML deficiencies.

On July 8, 2026, a proposed class action (Wong v. Toronto Dominion Bank and TD Securities Inc.) was filed in the Ontario Superior Court of Justice alleging that TD Bank and TD Securities failed to properly pay vacation and holiday pay on employees' incentive and other compensation under their Employee Incentive Programs, as required by statute.

TD Bank, N.A. and its parent company TD Bank US Holding Company pleaded guilty in October 2024 to conspiring to fail to maintain an anti-money laundering program, fail to file accurate Currency Transaction Reports, and launder monetary instruments. TD Bank agreed to pay $1.8 billion in penalties to the DOJ—the largest BSA penalty ever—and the total coordinated resolution with FinCEN and OCC reached almost $3.1 billion. The bank failed to maintain an effective AML program from January 2014 to October 2023, with 92% of transaction volume going unmonitored (~$18.3 trillion), enabling three money laundering networks to transfer more than $670 million through TD Bank accounts.

FinCEN assessed a record $1.3 billion civil penalty against TD Bank in October 2024 for willful violations of the Bank Secrecy Act, including failure to timely file SARs and failure to identify Da Ying Sze in more than 500 CTRs totaling more than $400 million in cash transactions from 2017 to 2021.

Wilfredo Aquino, a former TD Bank assistant store manager, pleaded guilty in January 2026 to conspiring to launder monetary instruments. From 2019 to February 2021, he facilitated a money laundering network's movement of approximately $474 million through TD Bank accounts and accepted over $11,000 in retail gift cards as bribes.

A TD Bank employee (Nunez) in Scotch Plains, New Jersey pleaded guilty in January 2026 to conspiring to launder monetary instruments and receiving bribes by a bank employee. From March 2021 to October 2023, he opened fraudulent shell company accounts, issued over 600 debit cards, and facilitated over $26 million in ATM withdrawals in Colombia.

Former TD Bank employee Leonardo Ayala pleaded guilty in January 2026 to conspiring to launder monetary instruments and receiving bribes by a bank employee. From June to November 2023, he opened fraudulent accounts, issued over 150 debit cards to shell companies, and facilitated approximately $5.5 million in ATM withdrawals in Colombia in exchange for over $6,000 in bribes.

Former TD Bank employee Gerardo Aquino pleaded guilty in October 2026 to conspiring to launder monetary instruments and receiving bribes by a bank employee, having laundered more than $4.8 million to Colombia while employed at TD Bank. Sentencing is scheduled for March 23, 2027.

OFAC announced a $115,005.04 settlement with TD Bank, N.A. for apparent violations of the North Korea Sanctions Regulations and the Foreign Narcotics Kingpin Sanctions Regulations. TDBNA processed 1,479 transactions totaling $382,685.38 and maintained nine accounts for employees of the North Korean mission to the UN without an OFAC license, and maintained accounts for a U.S. resident on OFAC's SDN list. The apparent violations were voluntarily self-disclosed and deemed non-egregious.

FinCEN assessed a record $1.3 billion civil penalty against TD Bank for chronic AML failures, including failure to detect and report suspicious activity involving high-risk jurisdictions and funnel account activity. The FinCEN consent order noted that a former TD Bank branch manager was suspected of colluding to circumvent reporting requirements and that TD Bank's investigation failed to escalate potential Cuba sanctions issues.

TD Bank, N.A. was charged in a criminal information in the District of New Jersey (Case 2:24-cr-00667-ES) with conspiracy to fail to maintain an adequate AML program and to file accurate Currency Transaction Reports, covering conduct from approximately January 2014 through October 2023. The indictment cited pervasive flaws in the Bank's transaction monitoring program and failures to identify and report suspicious activity, including activity involving high-risk jurisdictions.

TD Bank disclosed a data breach to the Massachusetts Office of Consumer Affairs and Business Regulation on September 15, 2026, involving unauthorized access to or disclosure of customers' personal and financial information. Exposed data included names, Social Security numbers, dates of birth, addresses, government-issued IDs, pay stubs, W-2s, financial account information, and credit/debit card numbers. At least 54 Massachusetts residents were identified as affected; the nationwide total was not disclosed. The bank is offering affected customers a complimentary two-year Fraud-Defender identity monitoring membership.

TD Bank reported a data breach to Massachusetts regulators in mid-June 2026 after discovering that an employee had unauthorized access to customer records between January 7 and January 30, 2026. The insider incident exposed names, addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth, Social Security numbers, account numbers, and transactional data of U.S. customers. A class action lawsuit was filed alleging negligence and inadequate data security practices.

TD Bank disclosed a data breach in February 2025 in which a former employee gained unauthorized access to customer information between August and December 2022. The incident was reported to Massachusetts regulators and affected at least eight Massachusetts residents; the nationwide total was not disclosed. TD Bank terminated the employee and worked with law enforcement to investigate.

NCB Management Services, a vendor partner of TD Bank, suffered a data breach beginning February 1, 2023, and detected by February 4, 2023, exploiting a misconfigured database. Over one million records were potentially accessed, including names, Social Security numbers, driver's license numbers, and bank account information, primarily affecting TD Bank customers. The breach prompted class action lawsuits and regulatory scrutiny, and TD Bank filed a data breach notice with the Maine Attorney General.

TD Bank's leadership knowingly presided over a criminally deficient anti-money laundering program between January 2014 and October 2023, allowing the bank to launder money for fentanyl and human trafficking rings. High-level executives, including the person who became the bank's chief AML officer, knew of serious problems but failed to correct them. DOJ charged only two relatively low-level employees while structuring penalties through the holding company (TD BHC) to avoid full liability on the bank and its executives.

TD Bank's compliance failures and the $3 billion fine suggest whistleblower involvement in building the government's case. The article notes that TD Bank ignored numerous warning signs and that DOJ may have been aided by insiders who came forward with evidence of the bank's massive transaction-monitoring gaps, highlighting governance and management failures to heed internal warnings.

CFPB Director Rohit Chopra stated that 'TD Bank's management clearly cared more about growth and expanding its empire through mergers' than treating customers fairly, criticizing leadership priorities in connection with the bank's illegal furnishing of inaccurate and fraudulent information to consumer reporting companies affecting hundreds of thousands of customers.
